newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's 1996 c/a deficit widens to $23.72 bln.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's 1996 c/a deficit widens to $23.72 bln.

text.p: South Korea's current account (C/A) deficit widened to a record $23.72 billion in 1996 from an $8.95 billion shortfall in 1995, preliminary figures from the Bank of Korea (BOK) showed on Sunday.
Note: figures are in millions of U.S. dollars
"Falling international prices for the nation's major exports were largely to blame for the 1996 deficit," said Kim Young-bae, assistant director of the bank's statistics division.
The BOK figures showed semiconductor price dropped by 61 percent, prices for chemical and steel products by 14.8 percent and eight percent, respectively.

A sharp rise in imports of consumer goods, crude and equipment related to information and telecommunications also contributed to the deficit, Kim said. Overall exports increased 4.1 percent in 1996, against a 31.5 percent rise in 1995, while imports rose 12.1 percent, against 32.1 percent.
Semiconductor exports on a customs-cleared basis fell to $17.8 billion in 1996 from $22.1 billion in 1995, and steel products dropped to $7.3 billion from $10 billion, the BOK figures showed.
Exports of heavy industrial goods rose a 0.9 percent in 1996 against a 37.5 percent rise in 1995, while light industrial products rose 7.5 percent, against a 14 percent rise.
Imports of foods and consumer goods increased 21.2 percent in 1996, crude rose 33.5 percent and precision equipment up 20.2 percent. "Import price for crude rose 15.9 percent last year," Kim said.
The BOK figures showed imports of capital goods rose 10 percent in 1996, compared with a 32.5 percent rise in 1995.
Imports of raw materials rose 10.2 percent, against last year's rise of 32.6 percent, the figures showed.
In the invisible trade account, payments rose to $38.33 billion in 1996 from $33.50 billion in 1995, while receipts increased to $30.65 billion from $29.86 billion.
The BOK earlier said the current account deficit would narrow this year to $18 billion.
